{{Short description|English banker}}
'''James Lockhart''' (1763–1852) was an English banker who wrote on [[numerical analysis]].<ref name="MNRAS">{{cite book|title=Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-bNBAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA112|year=1853|publisher=Priestley and Weale|pages=112–}}</ref>

==Life==
He was one of three children and two sons of James Lockhart (1735–1814), a Scottish banker, and his wife Mary Harriot Gray or Grey, from a Quaker family; [[John Ingram Lockhart]] was his brother, and the daughter was Mary Harriett, married name Greenwollers. He was educated at [[Reading School]] and [[Eton College]].<ref name="MNRAS"/><ref>{{cite book|title=The Gentleman's Magazine and Historical Review|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZlNFAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA198|year=1866|publisher=J.H. and J. Parker|page=198}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1790-1820/member/lockhart-john-ingram-1765-1835|title=''Lockhart, John Ingram'' (1765–1835), of Great Haseley, Oxon., History of Parliament Online|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000358/18511004/058/0001|title=To be premptorily sold|date=4 October 1851|work=Berkshire Chronicle|page=1|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref>

Lockhart worked as a banker in [[Pall Mall, London]], in his father's firm Lockhart, 
Wallace, & Co. He became a partner, and set up the Cattle Insurance Company.<ref name="MNRAS"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/cu31924030495000#page/n134/mode/1up|title=The Parliamentary History of the County of Oxford, including the city and university of Oxford, and the boroughs of Banbury, Burford, Chipping Norton, Dadington, Witney, and Woodstock, from the earliest times to the present day, 1213-1899, with biographical and genealogical notices of the members|last=Williams|first=William Retlaw|work=[[Internet Archive]]|year=1899 |publisher=Priv. Print. for the author by E. Davies|page=131|accessdate=6 April 2016|location=Brecknock}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=A Biographical Dictionary of the Living Authors of Great Britain and Ireland: Comprising Literary Memoirs and Anecdotes of Their Lives, and a Chronological Register of Their Publications, with the Number of Editions Printed; Including Notices of Some Foreign Writers Whose Works Have Been Occasionally Published in England|url=https://archive.org/details/b28146451|year=1816|publisher=Henry Colburn|page=[https://archive.org/details/b28146451/page/n221 208]}}</ref> Retiring from the bank in 1799, he moved north to the [[Windermere]] area after the death of his first wife.<ref name="MNRAS"/>

Lockhart knew [[Walking Stewart]], and stated he had learned from him. He knew also [[William Combe]], and the idea for Combe's "Dr Syntax" has been attributed to him. He taught mathematics to his own children, and pupils including [[Joshua King (mathematician)|Joshua King]].<ref name="MNRAS"/>

For about 15 years Lockhart and his family resided in the Netherlands, from 1819, in [[Leyden]] and then [[Haarlem]]. He returned to England on the death in 1835 of his brother John, who left no heir.<ref name="MNRAS"/>

Living first at [[Aylesbury]], Lockhart moved to the rectory at [[Cowley, Oxford|Cowley]] in 1837. After a legal case on his brother's will, the estate at Cowley was sold in 1841. He moved to [[Brompton, London|Brompton]].<ref name="MNRAS"/> In 1847 his address was given as Lanhams, near [[Braintree, Essex]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Memoirs of the Royal Astronomical Society|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5HOLOIgj4OAC&pg=PA573|year=1847|page=573}}</ref>

Taking a lease on shooting on the Scottish island of [[Raasay]], Lockhart spent time from 1845 on the [[Isle of Skye]]. He then lived in an [[Argyllshire]] mansion. He moved in 1851 to Clitsome House near [[Washford]] in Somerset.<ref name="MNRAS"/> He died there the following year.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Gentleman's Magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qBBIAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA215|year=1852|publisher=W. Pickering|page=215}}</ref>

==Works==
Lockhart proposed challenge problems on the separation of the roots of equations of degree five and six, some being published in 1841.<ref>{{cite book|title=The Mathematician|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=d_JJAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA165|year=1845|publisher=G. Bell|page=165}}</ref> He was still writing on the theory of equations while in Argyllshire.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Thomas Stephen Davies|author2=Stephen Fenwick|author3=William Rutheford|title=The Mathematician|url=https://archive.org/details/mathematician02ruthgoog|year=1850|publisher=G. Bell|page=[https://archive.org/details/mathematician02ruthgoog/page/n239 223]}}</ref> The challenges were considered by [[Florian Cajori]] to have influenced the work of [[John Radford Young]];<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/myxomycetescolo00sturgoog#page/n249/mode/1up|title=A History of the Arithmetical Methods of Approximation to the Roots of Numerical Equations of one Unknown Quantity Part III Modern Times|last=Cajori|first=Florian|year=1910|publisher=Colorado College|page=234|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref> [[William Rutherford (mathematician)|William Rutherford]] noted an analysis by Young of an equation proposed by Lockhart, in a book of 1849.<ref name="F.R.A.S.)1849">{{cite book|author=William Rutherford|title=The Complete Solution of Numerical Equations: in Which, by One Uniform Process, the Imaginary as Well as the Real Roots are Easily Determined|url=https://archive.org/details/b28754141|year=1849|page=[https://archive.org/details/b28754141/page/20 20]}}</ref>

Detailed analysis of a quintic using [[Budan's theorem]] for separation of roots was given in 1842, by James R. Christie;<ref>{{cite book|title=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VkYmsqL4EucC&pg=PA99|year=1842|publisher=Taylor & Francis|page=99}}</ref> it was noted by Young.<ref>{{cite book|author=J. R. Young|title=Researches respecting the Imaginary Roots of Numerical Equations|url=https://archive.org/details/researchesrespe00youngoog|year=1844|page=[https://archive.org/details/researchesrespe00youngoog/page/n59 55], note|publisher=Souter & Law }}</ref> In 1843 Young commented that Budan's approach, and Lockhart's own ideas, could now be simplified on the basis of recent developments, which had led to [[Sturm's theorem]].<ref>{{cite book|author=John Radford Young|title=Theory and Solution of Algebraical Equations of the Higher Orders|url=https://archive.org/details/theorysolutionof00younrich|year=1843|publisher=Souter and Law|page=[https://archive.org/details/theorysolutionof00younrich/page/245 245]}}</ref> Young also commended books by Lockhart in discussing a problem on roots proposed by [[John Pell (mathematician)|John Pell]] to [[Silius Titus]].<ref>{{cite book|author=John Radford Young|title=Mathematical Dissertations, for the Use of Students in the Modern Analysis|url=https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_McJuCH-6bYUC|year=1841|publisher=John Souter|pages=[https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_McJuCH-6bYUC/page/n177 159]–60 and notes|author-link=John Radford Young}}</ref> Lockhart and Young then influenced the subsequent work of [[Rehuel Lobatto]].<ref>{{cite book|title=The Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yJ9EAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA240|year=1862|page=240}}</ref>

Lockhart's books were mostly self-published:

*''A Method of Approximating Towards the Roots of Cubic Equations Belonging to the Irreducible Case'' (1813)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=A Method of Approximating Towards the Roots of Cubic Equations Belonging to the Irreducible Case|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yUQ1AQAAMAAJ|year=1813}}</ref>
*''Nieuwe en algemeene leerwijze om biquadraten op te lossen waarbij de systemas van Descartes en Euler tot biquadraten met derzelver tweede termen worden voortgezet'' (1823)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=Nieuwe en algemeene leerwijze om biquadraten op te lossen waarbij de systemas van Descartes en Euler tot biquadraten met derzelver tweede termen worden voortgezet|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lGBhAAAAcAAJ|year=1823}}</ref>
*''Nieuwe oplossing van cubiek-vergelykingen door juiste uitdrukkingen, en ook bij nadering, zonder beproeving of gissing'' (1825)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=Nieuwe oplossing van cubiek-vergelykingen door juiste uitdrukkingen, en ook bij nadering, zonder beproeving of gissing|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5V9hAAAAcAAJ|year=1825|publisher=erven François Bohn}}</ref>
*''Extension of the celebrated theorem of C. Sturm, whereby the roots of numeral equations may be separated from each other, with copious examples'' (1839)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=Extension of the celebrated theorem of C. Sturm, whereby the roots of numeral equations may be separated from each other, with copious examples|url=https://archive.org/details/extensionofceleb00lockrich|page=[https://archive.org/details/extensionofceleb00lockrich/page/n27 1]|year=1839|publisher=the Author}}</ref>
*''Resolution of Two Equations'' (1839)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=Resolution of Two Equations. Being a homage to the memory of the founders and benefactors of the University of Oxford, at the Commemoration held on the 12th of June, 1839|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zh1hAAAAcAAJ|year=1839|publisher=the Author}}</ref>
*''Resolution of Equations by Means of Inferior and Superior Limits'' (1842)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=Resolution of Equations by Means of Inferior and Superior Limits|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vwZLcgAACAAJ|year=1842|publisher=Lockhart}}</ref>
*''The Nature of the Roots of Numerical Equations'' (1850)<ref>{{cite book|author=James Lockhart|title=The Nature of the Roots of Numerical Equations|publisher=C. and J. Adlard|url=https://archive.org/details/naturerootsnume00lockgoog|year=1850}}</ref>

==Family==
Lockhart married twice. With his first wife, Mary Coxe, daughter of Leonard Coxe of [[Philadelphia]], a dispossessed loyalist of the [[American Revolution]], he had three daughters and a son.<ref name="MNRAS"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/countyfamiliesof42walf#page/593/mode/1up|title=The County Families of the United Kingdom; or, Royal manual of the titled and untitled aristocracy of England, Wales, Scotland, and Ireland ..|last=Walford|first=Edward|year=1868|work=[[Internet Archive]]|publisher=R. Hardwicke|pages=593|volume=2|location=London|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref> With his second wife Elizabeth, whom he married in 1805, he had six sons and two daughters; she died in 1843 at age 56.<ref name="MNRAS"/><ref>{{cite book|title=The Gentleman's Magazine|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o2Q3AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA104|year=1843|publisher=F. Jefferies|page=104}}</ref> Lockhart's children included:

*James, the eldest son, a barrister and poet;<ref>[[s:Page:Men-at-the-Bar.djvu/319]]</ref><ref name="Reilly2000">{{cite book|author=Catherine Reilly|title=Mid-Victorian Poetry, 1860-1879|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bzRDJeN4KxQC&pg=PA280|year=2000|publisher=A&C Black|isbn=978-0-7201-2318-0|page=280}}</ref> James Augustus Lockhart, officer in the [[41st (Welsh) Regiment of Foot|41st Regiment]], killed at age 21 on 8 September 1855 in the [[Crimean War]] was his son.<ref>{{cite book|author=Henry Press Wright|title=The Story of the "Domus Dei" of Portsmouth, Commonly Called The Royal Garrison Church|url=https://archive.org/details/storyofdomusdeio00wrig|year=1873|publisher=J. Parker|page=[https://archive.org/details/storyofdomusdeio00wrig/page/78 78]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000231/18551027/046/0005|title=The Late Captain Lockhart|date=27 October 1855|work=Hampshire Chronicle|page=5|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref>
*[[John Ingram Lockhart (writer)|John Ingram]] (1812–1889), a writer and friend of [[Nicolaas Beets]].<ref>{{cite web|language=nl|url=http://www.dbnl.org/tekst/beet005pete01_01/beet005pete01_01_0025.php#106T|title=Nicolaas Beets, Het dagboek van de student Nicolaas Beets, 1833-1836 · dbnl|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref>
*Miles, who married Anna Rebecca Charlotte, daughter of Major Robert Stewart of the [[94th Regiment of Foot|94th Regiment]];<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/stewartsofappin00stew#page/150/mode/1up/search/Miles|title=Stewarts of Appin|last=Stewart|first=John H. J.|year=1880|work=[[Internet Archive]]|publisher=Maclachlan & Stewart|page=150|accessdate=6 April 2016|location=Edinburgh}}</ref> [[James Haldane Stewart Lockhart]] was their son.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/stream/whoswhoinfareast00hongrich#page/204/mode/1up|title=Who's who in the Far East, 1906–7, June|year=1906|work=[[Internet Archive]]|publisher=China Mail|page=204|accessdate=6 April 2016|location=Hongkong}}</ref>
*Maria, who married John Smith of [[Ellingham Hall, Norfolk]] in 1828.<ref>'Parishes: Sherfield English', in ''A History of the County of Hampshire'': Volume 4, ed. William Page (London, 1911), pp. 510–511. British History Online http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/hants/vol4/pp510-511 [accessed 6 April 2016].</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000858/18280529/032/0003|title=Marriages|date=29 May 1828|work=Westmeath Journal|page=3|accessdate=6 April 2016}}</ref>
